front: What is shared by all branches of an RLC parallel circuit?
back: The voltage.

front: Phase of each branch current vs voltage?
back: Resistor: in phase. Inductor: lags 90°. Capacitor: leads 90°.

front: How are Iₗ and Ic related in parallel?
back: 180° apart — they subtract (cancel).

front: When is a parallel RLC circuit lagging vs leading?
back: More inductive VARs/current → lagging. More capacitive → leading.

front: In parallel, does the bigger or smaller reactance win?
back: The SMALLER reactance draws more current and dominates (reverse of series).
extra_notes: Xl 8 Ω vs Xc 16 Ω → inductive

front: Branch currents for 12 Ω ∥ Xl 8 Ω ∥ Xc 16 Ω on 240 V?
back: Iᵣ 20 A, Iₗ 30 A, Ic 15 A.

front: Total current formula for RLC parallel?
back: Iₜ = √(Iᵣ² + (Iₗ − Ic)²)

front: Iᵣ 20, Iₗ 30, Ic 15 A. Iₜ?
Can a branch carry more current than the line?
back: Yes — the 30 A coil branch exceeds the 25 A line current, because Ic cancels part of Iₗ.

front: Iᵣ 38, Iₗ 22, Ic 7 A. Iₜ?
Simplest way to find Z in RLC parallel?
Reciprocal formula for RLC parallel impedance?
extra_notes: Subtract the RECIPROCALS of Xl and Xc

front: Second impedance method (combine reactances first)?
back: X = Xl·Xc / (Xl + Xc) with Xc NEGATIVE; then Z = R·X/√(R² + X²). 8×(−16)/(8−16) = 16 Ω → Z = 9.6 Ω.

front: Example 24–2: R 18 Ω, 9.76 mH, 5.5 µF at 1200 Hz. First step and Z?
back: Xl = 73.59 Ω, Xc = 24.11 Ω (377 doesn't apply); Z ≈ 16.1 Ω.

front: Power values in Example 24–1?
back: P 4800 W; VARsL 7200; VARsC 3600; VA 6000.

front: Apparent power formula for RLC parallel?
back: VA = √(P² + (VARsL − VARsC)²)

front: Example 24–1 PF and θ?
PF formulas in parallel RLC?
back: P/VA, Iᵣ/Iₜ, Z/R

front: L and C in Example 24–1?
What is a tank circuit?
back: An L-C parallel (resonant) circuit, in which energy swings back and forth between the coil and capacitor.

front: At parallel resonance, what happens to impedance and line current?
back: Impedance is MAXIMUM; line current is MINIMUM.

front: Compare series and parallel resonance.
back: Series: Z min, current max, voltage magnified. Parallel: Z max, line current min, circulating current magnified.

front: What limits the line current of a real tank circuit?
back: The resistance (Q) of the coil — capacitors have very high Q.
extra_notes: Ideal: zero line current, infinite Z

front: Q of a tank circuit — two formulas?
back: Q = Xl/R = I(tank)/I(line)

front: 0.0398 H (10 Ω), 0.442 µF on 480 V at 1200 Hz: tank current, Q and line current?
Check the tank line current using power.
Impedance of that tank at resonance?
back: 480/0.0533 ≈ 9000 Ω (book's 9006 comes from rounding).

front: Tank Xl = Xc = 30 Ω, coil Q = 15, 277 V. Line current?
Bandwidth of a parallel resonant circuit?
back: Frequency range where impedance is ≥ 0.707 × maximum; high Q = narrow, low Q = wide.

front: Pitfall: "tiny line current, so L and C are lightly loaded"?
back: Wrong — each carries the full circulating tank current (Q × line current).

front: How does an induction heater use a tank circuit?
back: The work coil (with the pipe as core) and a capacitor resonate; I(tank) = Q × I(line) — Q 10: 100 A line → 1000 A heating current.

front: Induction heating: low vs high frequency?
back: ≤ 400 Hz heats evenly through; ≥ 1000 Hz skin effect heats the surface (case hardening).

front: Why is an induction heater only resonant with the part in the coil?
back: The part acts as the coil's core, so it changes L.

front: How does an inductive proximity sensor use a tank circuit?
back: Metal near the face adds eddy-current losses, Q collapses, the oscillation stops, and the sensor switches.

front: C to resonate with 0.796 mH (Xl 50 Ω) at 10 kHz?
Why can a capacitor correct a motor's power factor?
back: In parallel, its leading current cancels much of the motor's lagging magnetizing current, so the line carries less.

front: How does a motor look electrically at no load vs full load?
back: R in series with L; L (magnetizing) stays ~constant, R grows with load → low PF at no load, higher at full load.

front: PF correction step 1–2 (240 V, 10 A, 1630 W)?
PF correction step 3–4 (target 95%)?
PF correction step 5–7?
back: VARsC = 1761.6 − 535.8 = 1225.8; Xc = 240²/1225.8 = 46.99 Ω; C = 1/(377 × 46.99) = 56.45 µF in parallel.

front: After correcting that motor to 95%, what's the line current?
back: ≈ 1715.8/240 = 7.15 A (down from 10 A). The motor's own current is unchanged.

front: Formula for Xc from required capacitive VARs?
back: Xc = E² / VARsC

front: To correct to unity (100%), how many VARsC?
back: Equal to all the existing inductive VARs.

front: Why correct to ~95% rather than 100%?
back: Diminishing returns — each extra point needs more kVAR; overshooting makes PF leading and raises voltage.

front: Does corrected PF stay constant at all motor loads?
back: No (despite the book). Watts drop at light load, so PF falls; an oversized capacitor can overcorrect.

front: Book error in PF correction step 5?
back: It says reduce VARs "from 1715.789" — that's VA. The existing VARs are 1761.562. Also "PF = 0679" should be 0.679.

front: NEC limits for a capacitor on the load side of a motor overload?
back: kVAR ≤ the amount to raise no-load PF to unity (460.7, avoids self-excitation); set overloads on the reduced current (460.9).

front: Why can PF banks cause harmonic problems in plants with drives?
back: Bank + system inductance form a tank circuit; near a harmonic its high impedance magnifies harmonic voltage/current. Use detuned banks.

front: Practical: 240 V, 15 A, 2.2 kW motor to 95%. Method?
back: VA = 3600 → PF ≈ 61%; VARs now = √(3600² − 2200²); target VA = 2200/0.95; VARs target; difference = VARsC; Xc = 240²/VARsC; C = 1/(377·Xc).
